## Observations

1. For a fixed string, each operation is determined by its three letters and covers the two positions at its start and immediately after it. Two consecutive starts cannot both support operations, because the second character of one triple must be `R` while the first character of the next must be `A` or `C`.
2. A matching of covering pairs leaves a gap of at least three between some consecutive starts in cyclic order exactly when it is nonempty and leaves a position unmatched.
3. Consecutive starts two positions apart share a triple endpoint, so their triples must alternate between `ARC` and `CRA`.
4. On an odd cycle, removing one position leaves an even-length path. On an even cycle, every matching edge covers one odd and one even position.

## Solution sketch

> For a fixed string, each operation is determined by its three letters and covers the two positions at its start and immediately after it. Two consecutive starts cannot both support operations, because the second character of one triple must be `R` while the first character of the next must be `A` or `C`.

1. Treat the covering pairs as edges of the cycle. Any good string supplies a matching that covers every zero, since two such edges share a vertex only if their starts are consecutive. The operations only set entries to 1, so their order is immaterial. Print `Yes` immediately if there are no zeros, since the empty matching suffices.

> A matching of covering pairs leaves a gap of at least three between some consecutive starts in cyclic order exactly when it is nonempty and leaves a position unmatched.

2. Any nonempty matching with an unmatched position can be realized by a string. Start just after a gap of at least three and traverse the selected starts in cyclic order. At each gap of two, use the opposite triple from the previous start so the shared endpoint gets the same letter. At each gap of at least three, either triple can be used because the triples do not overlap across that gap. The initial gap prevents a conflict when the traversal wraps around. Fill any unspecified positions arbitrarily.

> Consecutive starts two positions apart share a triple endpoint, so their triples must alternate between `ARC` and `CRA`.

3. In a perfect matching, every gap is two, so the alternation must close around the cycle. This is possible exactly when the number of selected edges, \(N/2\), is even. Therefore, if \(N\) is divisible by four, print `Yes` regardless of the input bits.

> On an odd cycle, removing one position leaves an even-length path. On an even cycle, every matching edge covers one odd and one even position.

4. If \(N\) is odd, print `Yes` exactly when there is at least one 1. Leave that position unmatched and pair consecutive vertices along the remaining path. If every position is zero, a perfect matching would be necessary, which is impossible on an odd cycle. This also handles \(N=3\).
5. If \(N\) is even and has remainder two modulo four, print `Yes` exactly when there is a 1 at both an odd and an even position. A realizable matching must leave a position unmatched in this case. Since each edge uses one position of each parity, it must leave at least one of each parity unmatched, and both must already be 1. Conversely, removing one such position of each parity leaves two paths with even numbers of vertices, either of which can be empty. Pair consecutive vertices along both paths to obtain a realizable matching.
6. Scan the sequence once, recording whether any zero exists and whether a 1 occurs at each parity. The decision takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond input storage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
